claim: Mutations or genetic variation in noncoding regions of the genome harbouring cis-regulatory elements (CREs), or enhancers, have been widely implicated in human disease and disease risk.
source: Mutations or genetic variation in noncoding regions of the genome harbouring cis-regulatory elements (CREs), or enhancers, have been widely implicated in human disease and disease risk.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bhatia and Kleinjan, 2014; Chatterjee and Ahituv, 2017) as indicated in the full text.

claim: Q-STARZ allows simultaneous quantitative assessment of the spatial and temporal activity of wild-type and disease-associated mutant human CRE alleles using live imaging in zebrafish embryonic development.
source: Here, we describe a method for simultaneous quantitative assessment of the spatial and temporal activity of wild-type and disease-associated mutant human CRE alleles using live imaging in zebrafish embryonic development.
evidence: This is the primary methodological claim of the manuscript, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the Results section.

claim: Transgenic lines harbour a dual-CRE dual-reporter cassette in a pre-defined neutral docking site in the zebrafish genome.
source: We generated transgenic lines harbouring a dual-CRE dual-reporter cassette in a pre-defined neutral docking site in the zebrafish genome.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The activity of each CRE allele is reported via expression of a specific fluorescent reporter, allowing simultaneous visualisation of where and when in development the wild-type allele is active and how this activity is altered by mutation.
source: The activity of each CRE allele is reported via expression of a specific fluorescent reporter, allowing simultaneous visualisation of where and when in development the wild-type allele is active and how this activity is altered by mutation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figures 4 and 5, showing fluorescent reporter expression patterns.

claim: Disease-associated sequence variation in enhancers can alter transcription factor (TF) binding sites, leading to aberrant enhancer function and altered target gene expression.
source: Disease-associated sequence variation in enhancers can alter transcription factor (TF) binding sites, leading to aberrant enhancer function and altered target gene expression (Bhatia and Kleinjan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Incomplete understanding of the TF binding potential of CREs impedes functional assessment of pathogenicity of genetic variants in the noncoding genome.
source: However, compared to coding regions where the functional consequence of genetic variants can be extrapolated from knowledge about protein's structure and function, incomplete understanding of the TF binding potential of CREs impedes functional assessment of pathogenicity of genetic variants in the noncoding genome.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about the challenges in noncoding genome interpretation.

claim: Functional analysis of enhancer activity depends on the availability of the right TFs in the right stoichiometric concentrations, which is only precisely captured in vivo.
source: Functional analysis of enhancer activity, and assessing the impact of disease-associated variation on this activity, depends on the availability of the right TFs in the right stoichiometric concentrations, which is only precisely captured in vivo.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about enhancer function and the importance of in vivo context.

claim: Enhancer-reporter transgenic assays have been widely employed in a variety of model organisms, including the mouse, to assess enhancer function in vivo.
source: Enhancer-reporter transgenic assays have been widely employed in a variety of model organisms, including the mouse, to assess enhancer function in vivo (Ashery-Padan and Gruss, 2001; Bhatia et al., 2015; Farley et al., 2015; Rogers and Williams, 2011; Visel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Conventional enhancer-reporter assays can be affected by the random integration of transgenes.
source: These assays however can be affected by the random integration of transgenes and have limited application for studying the temporal aspects of enhancer function over the time course of embryonic development since, for example, live imaging is challenging due to the opaqueness of the mouse embryo and its in utero embryonic development.
evidence: This is based on known limitations of conventional transgenic approaches.

claim: Live imaging is challenging in mouse embryos due to their opaqueness and in utero embryonic development.
source: These assays however can be affected by the random integration of transgenes and have limited application for studying the temporal aspects of enhancer function over the time course of embryonic development since, for example, live imaging is challenging due to the opaqueness of the mouse embryo and its in utero embryonic development.
evidence: This is based on known biological characteristics of mouse embryonic development.

claim: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) is a highly suitable in vivo vertebrate model for visualising tissue-specific enhancer activity.
source: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) is a highly suitable in vivo vertebrate model for visualising tissue-specific enhancer activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about zebrafish as a model organism.

claim: Robust transgenesis methods allow rapid generation of transgenic zebrafish lines yielding transparent embryos which develop externally.
source: Robust transgenesis methods allow rapid generation of transgenic lines yielding transparent embryos which develop externally (Mann and Bhatia, 2019; Phillips and Westerfield, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The activities of a large number of putative human and mouse CREs have been assessed in transgenic zebrafish models, irrespective of the primary sequence conservation of the mammalian CREs in zebrafish.
source: The activities of a large number of putative human and mouse CREs have been assessed in transgenic zebrafish models, irrespective of the primary sequence conservation of the mammalian CREs in zebrafish (Bhatia et al., 2013; Bhatia et al., 2015; Chahal et al., 2019; Goode and Elgar, 2013; Rainger et al., 2014; Ravi et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Conventional zebrafish assays based on Tol2 recombination mediate random integration of the CRE-reporter cassette in the zebrafish genome.
source: However, these assays were based on Tol2 recombination which mediates random integration of the CRE-reporter cassette in the zebrafish genome (Kawakami et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Measured CRE activities in conventional Tol2-based assays were strongly influenced by the variable site and copy number of integrations.
source: The measured CRE activities were strongly influenced by the variable site and copy number of integrations, necessitating analysis of each element in multiple transgenic lines and precluding quantitative assessment of CRE activities.
evidence: This is based on known limitations of Tol2-mediated transgenesis.

claim: Position effect biases can be alleviated by targeted integration of the transgenic cassette into pre-defined neutral sites in the zebrafish genome using phiC31-mediated recombination.
source: These biases can be alleviated by targeted integration of the transgenic cassette into pre-defined neutral sites in the zebrafish genome using phiC31-mediated recombination (Hadzhiev et al., 2016; Mosimann et al., 2013; Roberts et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A previous dual fluorescence CRE-reporter zebrafish transgenic system allowed for direct comparison of the in vivo spatial and temporal activity of wild-type and mutant CREs in the same developing embryo.
source: Previously, we developed a system in which dual fluorescence CRE-reporter zebrafish transgenics allow for direct comparison of the in vivo spatial and temporal activity of wild-type (Wt) and putative SNP/mutation (Mut) bearing CREs in the same developing embryo (Bhatia et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The previous dual fluorescence system was not suitable for quantitative assessment of altered CRE activity because CRE alleles were on separate constructs randomly integrated into the zebrafish genome.
source: However, as the CRE alleles were on separate constructs randomly integrated into the zebrafish genome, the assay was not suitable for quantitative assessment of altered CRE activity.
evidence: This is based on the authors' assessment of limitations in their previous method.

claim: Q-STARZ is based upon targeted integration of a dual-CRE dual-reporter cassette into a pre-defined site in the zebrafish genome.
source: Here we describe Q-STARZ (Quantitative Spatial and Temporal Assessment of Regulatory element activity in Zebrafish), a new and significantly improved design of our previous transgenic reporter assay, based upon targeted integration of a dual-CRE dual-reporter cassette into a pre-defined site in the zebrafish genome (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental design shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Q-STARZ transgenic cassette contains both Wt and mutant CREs, separated by strong insulator sequences, with the transcriptional potential of both CREs read out as expression of different fluorescent proteins.
source: A unique feature of this design is the single transgenic cassette containing both Wt and mutant CREs, separated by strong insulator sequences, with the transcriptional potential of both CREs read out as expression of different fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the construct design shown in Figure 1 and experimental validation in Figure 3.

claim: Q-STARZ allows robust, unbiased assessment of spatial and temporal activities of both CREs using a single transgenic line, thereby reducing animal usage by up to 75% compared to the previous design.
source: This allows robust, unbiased assessment of spatial and temporal activities of both CREs using a single transgenic line, thereby reducing animal usage by up to 75% compared to the previous design.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the previous method and the improved design.

claim: Landing pads containing phiC31 attB integration sites were integrated at random sites in the zebrafish genome using Tol2-mediated transgenesis.
source: Using Tol2-mediated transgenesis, we integrated 'landing pads' at random sites in the zebrafish genome (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental procedure described and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Landing pads contain 'tracking CREs' driving expression of a 'tracking reporter gene' to visualise successful integration events.
source: To visualise successful integration events, the landing pads contain 'tracking CREs' (Supplementary file 1) driving expression of a 'tracking reporter gene'.
evidence: This is part of the experimental design described in the Methods.

claim: CRE activities were observed to be highly influenced by the site of integration in F1 embryos derived from founder lines bearing SOX9-CNEa and Pax6-SIMO CREs.
source: CRE activities were observed to be highly influenced by the site of integration in F1 embryos derived from founder lines bearing SOX9-CNEa and Pax6-SIMO CREs (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Three independent landing lines with a clean eGFP expression pattern were obtained using Shh-SBE2 as the tracking CRE.
source: but we obtained three independent landing lines with a clean eGFP expression pattern using Shh-SBE2 as the tracking CRE (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Shh-SBE2 is a forebrain enhancer driving Shh expression in the hypothalamus.
source: Shh-SBE2 is a forebrain enhancer driving Shh expression in the hypothalamus (Jeong and Epstein, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The precise integration site of the landing pad in the three Shh-SBE2 lines was determined using ligation-mediated PCR (LM-PCR) and transgene segregation analysis.
source: The precise integration site of the landing pad in the three Shh-SBE2 lines was determined using ligation-mediated PCR (LM-PCR) and transgene segregation analysis (described in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The Shh-SBE2 landing line with a clean single-site integration was used for all subsequent experiments.
source: Based on these observations, we decided to use the Shh-SBE2 landing line with a clean single-site integration for all subsequent experiments described in this study (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological decision based on the characterization data.

claim: The chicken β-globin 5′HS4 (cHS4) insulator sequence was placed between the two CRE-reporter cassettes to prevent crosstalk between the two enhancers.
source: In order to prevent crosstalk between the two enhancers, a well-characterised insulator sequence from the chicken genome, chicken β-globin 5′HS4 (cHS4) (Chung et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1997), was placed between the two CRE-reporter cassettes (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing the insulator and demonstrated in the construct design.

claim: PAX6-7CE3 drives expression in the hindbrain and neural tube from 24 to 120 hr post fertilisation (hpf).
source: PAX6-7CE3 drives expression in the hindbrain and neural tube from 24 to 120 hr post fertilisation (hpf), while PAX6-SIMO activity is in developing lens and forebrain from 48 to 120 hpf (Bhatia et al., 2013; Ravi et al., 2013; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and demonstrated in the current study.

claim: PAX6-SIMO activity is in developing lens and forebrain from 48 to 120 hpf.
source: PAX6-7CE3 drives expression in the hindbrain and neural tube from 24 to 120 hr post fertilisation (hpf), while PAX6-SIMO activity is in developing lens and forebrain from 48 to 120 hpf (Bhatia et al., 2013; Ravi et al., 2013; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and demonstrated in the current study.

claim: When the two CRE-reporter cassettes were separated by a 'neutral' sequence with no insulator activity, complete crosstalk of the two CRE activities was observed.
source: When the two CRE-reporter cassettes were separated by a 'neutral' sequence – a randomly selected region from the mouse genome with no insulator activity – we observed complete crosstalk of the two CRE activities (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant difference in CRE activities was observed in the dye-swap experiment, indicating no bias was introduced by varying signal intensities from the two fluorophores used.
source: We also performed a dye-swap experiment wherein the eGFP and mCherry reporters were swapped between the two CREs. We observed no significant difference in CRE activities in the dye-swap experiment, indicating no bias was introduced by varying signal intensities from the two fluorophores used (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Crosstalk between the two enhancer-reporter cassettes was progressively reduced with increasing copies of cHS4, with complete insulation achieved in replacement cassettes bearing three copies (3xcHS4).
source: Crosstalk between the two enhancer-reporter cassettes was progressively reduced with increasing copies of cHS4, with complete insulation achieved in replacement cassettes bearing three copies (3xcHS4) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: As the number of copies of the insulator increases, there is progressively restricted expression of the reporters towards expression only in the activity domains of their associated CRE.
source: This analysis confirmed that, as the number of copies of the insulator increases, there is progressively restricted expression of the reporters towards expression only in the activity domains of their associated CRE (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Shh-SBE2 and Shh-SBE4 have been previously demonstrated to have highly similar domains of activity in the developing forebrain of mouse embryos.
source: To establish proof of principle, we investigated the precise spatial and temporal activities of two CREs from the Shh locus, Shh-SBE2 and Shh-SBE4, previously demonstrated to have highly similar domains of activity in the developing forebrain of mouse embryos (Figure 4; Jeong and Epstein, 2003; Jeong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Shh-SBE2 and Shh-SBE4 have unique, as well as overlapping, domains of activity in the early stages of forebrain development (~24–50 hpf).
source: Our analyses revealed unique, as well as overlapping, domains of activity of both CREs in the early stages of forebrain development (~24–50 hpf) (Figure 4, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Video 1.

claim: From ~60 to 120 hpf, the activities of Shh-SBE2 and Shh-SBE4 are in completely distinct domains of the developing forebrain with no overlapping activity observed.
source: However, from ~60 to 120 hpf, the activities of both CREs are in completely distinct domains of the developing forebrain with no overlapping activity observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Video 2.

claim: Shh-SBE2 was active in the rostral part of forebrain while Shh-SBE4 activity was restricted to caudal forebrain from ~60 to 120 hpf.
source: Shh-SBE2 was active in the rostral part of forebrain while Shh-SBE4 activity was restricted to caudal forebrain (Figure 4, Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 4 and Video 2.

claim: A point mutation (C>T) in SBE2 was identified in a patient with holoprosencephaly and shown to abrogate the activity of SBE2 in the rostral hypothalamus of the mouse.
source: We tested this in SBE2, a regulatory element that controls SHH expression in the developing forebrain, using a point mutation (C>T) identified in a patient with holoprosencephaly and shown to abrogate the activity of SBE2 in the rostral hypothalamus of the mouse (Figure 5; Bhatia et al., 2015; Jeong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No difference in the activities of the wild-type and mutant SBE2 alleles was detected in very early development until ~40 hpf.
source: We detected no difference in the activities of the two alleles in very early development until ~40 hpf.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: From ~48 to 72 hpf, activity of the wild-type and mutant SBE2 alleles started to diverge.
source: However, from ~48 to 72 hpf, activity of the alleles started to diverge.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: Expression driven by the wild-type SBE2 allele was observed in the developing rostral and caudal hypothalamus of transgenic embryos while the mutant allele was only active in the caudal hypothalamus.
source: Expression driven by the Wt allele was observed in the developing rostral and caudal hypothalamus of transgenic embryos while the Mut allele was only active in the caudal hypothalamus, indicating that the mutation disrupts rostral activity of the SBE2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mutation in SBE2 disrupts rostral activity of the enhancer.
source: Expression driven by the Wt allele was observed in the developing rostral and caudal hypothalamus of transgenic embryos while the Mut allele was only active in the caudal hypothalamus, indicating that the mutation disrupts rostral activity of the SBE2.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression patterns observed between wild-type and mutant alleles.

claim: No significant difference in activity between the wild-type and mutant SBE2 alleles was observed at 28 hpf.
source: Upon quantification of reporter gene expression associated with each allele, we observed no significant difference in activity between the two alleles at 28 hpf.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: At later stages of development (48 and 72 hpf), the mutant SBE2 allele failed to drive reporter gene expression in the rostral hypothalamus and had significantly weaker activity in the caudal hypothalamus.
source: However, at later stages of development (48 and 72 hpf), the mutant allele failed to drive reporter gene expression in the rostral hypothalamus and had significantly weaker activity in the caudal hypothalamus (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The noncoding region of the human genome is estimated to contain approximately 1 million enhancers.
source: The noncoding region of the human genome is estimated to contain approximately 1 million enhancers (Consortium, 2012; Thurman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing combined with genome-wide identification of chromatin signatures has led to the identification of a large number of putative enhancers with disease-associated or disease risk-associated sequence variation.
source: The widespread application of whole-genome sequencing for understanding genetic diseases (rare, common and acquired – i.e. cancer), combined with genome-wide identification of chromatin signatures associated with active enhancers, has led to the identification of a large number of putative enhancers with disease-associated or disease risk-associated sequence variation (Bhatia and Kleinjan, 2014; Chatterjee and Ahituv, 2017; Short et al., 2018; Wu and Pan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Q-STARZ is highly versatile and enables unambiguous assessment of human tissue-specific CRE function in vivo at all stages of early embryonic development in a vertebrate model system.
source: The Q-STARZ assay we describe here is highly versatile and enables unambiguous assessment of human tissue-specific CRE function in vivo at all stages of early embryonic development in a vertebrate model system.
evidence: This is based on the experimental demonstrations throughout the Results section.

claim: Q-STARZ enables direct comparisons of activities of wild-type and mutant alleles inside the same, transparent developing embryo using live imaging.
source: Q-STARZ however offers a unique advantage when analysing the effects of disease-associated sequence variation on CRE function by enabling direct comparisons of activities of Wt and mutant alleles inside the same, transparent developing embryo using live imaging.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Docking the dual-CRE dual-reporter cassette into a pre-defined site in the zebrafish genome ensures no variability in transgene expression patterns.
source: Docking the dual-CRE dual-reporter cassette into a pre-defined site in the zebrafish genome ensures no variability in transgene expression patterns.
evidence: This is inferred from the targeted integration approach and the consistent expression patterns observed.

claim: Inclusion of three tandem copies of a strong insulator sequence robustly prevents crosstalk between the two CREs analysed.
source: Using CREs with previously well-established activities, we demonstrate that inclusion of three tandem copies of a strong insulator sequence in the a construct robustly prevents crosstalk between the two CREs analysed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Q-STARZ can uncover the precise sites and time points in embryonic development where CRE functions are unique and where they overlap with each other.
source: We demonstrate here that this can uncover the precise sites and time points in embryonic development where the CRE functions are unique and where they overlap with each other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis of Shh-SBE2 and Shh-SBE4 shown in Figure 4.

claim: Q-STARZ is an ideal tool for generating a detailed cell-type-specific view of CRE usage during embryonic development.
source: Q-STARZ is therefore an ideal tool for generating a detailed cell-type-specific view of CRE usage during embryonic development.
evidence: This is inferred from the capabilities demonstrated in the Results section.

claim: Analysis of CREs from PAX6 and SHH loci in conventional transgenic assays has revealed multiple CREs apparently driving target gene expression in the same or highly overlapping tissues and cell types.
source: Analysis of CREs derived from these loci in conventional transgenic assays has revealed multiple CREs apparently driving target gene expression in the same or highly overlapping tissues and cell types.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies of these loci.

claim: The concept of redundancy in enhancer function has been proposed to confer robustness of expression upon genes with key roles in embryonic development.
source: This has led to the concept of redundancy in enhancer function conferring robustness of expression upon genes with key roles in embryonic development (Cannavò et al., 2016; Frankel et al., 2010; Osterwalder et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Analysis of Shh-SBE2 and SBE4 enhancers reveals subtly distinct spatial and temporal activity domains of each enhancer during development.
source: However, our analysis of the Shh-SBE2 and SBE4 enhancers, previously reported as forebrain enhancers with overlapping functions, reveals subtly distinct spatial and temporal activity domains of each enhancer during development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There are small but important differences in the timing of action or precise localisation in cell types within the forebrain where Shh-SBE2 and SBE4 enhancers exert their roles that are overlooked when analysed independently in conventional transgenic assays.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesise that there are small but important differences in the timing of action or precise localisation in cell types within the forebrain where these enhancers exert their roles that are overlooked when analysed independently in conventional transgenic assays.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations from the Q-STARZ analysis.

claim: Live imaging of transgenic embryos carrying a reporter cassette with a previously validated disease-associated point mutation in the SHH-SBE2 enhancer revealed the loss of activity of the mutant allele in the rostral hypothalamus compared to the wild-type CRE.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that Q-STARZ can robustly detect differences in activities of mutant and Wt CRE alleles. Live imaging of transgenic embryos carrying a reporter cassette with a previously validated disease-associated point mutation in the SHH-SBE2 enhancer revealed the loss of activity of the mutant allele in the rostral hypothalamus compared to the Wt CRE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The loss of rostral activity of the SBE2 mutant has been previously reported in mouse transgenic assays.
source: This recapitulates a similar loss of rostral activity of the SBE2 mutant that has been previously reported in mouse transgenic assays (Jeong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Q-STARZ enabled determination of the precise time point in development when the mutation affects CRE function by visualising the activities of both the wild-type and mutant alleles simultaneously in the same embryos in real time.
source: However, since we could visualise the activities of both the Wt and mutant alleles simultaneously in the same embryos in real time, we were able to determine the precise time point in development when the mutation affects CRE function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Q-STARZ could significantly improve our ability to discern potentially pathogenic and functional sequence variation from background human genetic variation.
source: We propose that Q-STARZ will be a powerful tool to define the precise cell types and stages of development where CRE function is affected by mutations or SNPs identified by GWAS and other studies, thus this could significantly improve our ability to discern potentially pathogenic and functional sequence variation from background human genetic variation, which is currently a major challenge for human genetics.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential future applications of the method.

claim: The Q-STARZ analysis pipeline would only be suitable for CREs associated with genes active in early stages of embryonic development.
source: The analysis pipeline would only be suitable for CREs associated with genes active in early stages of embryonic development.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the developmental stages accessible in the zebrafish model.

claim: PAX6 is a transcription factor with vital pleiotropic roles in embryonic development.
source: PAX6 is a TF with vital pleiotropic roles in embryonic development (Ashery-Padan and Gruss, 2001; Kleinjan and van Heyningen, 2005; Osumi et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: More than 30 CREs have been characterised which coordinate precise spatial and temporal PAX6 expression in the developing eyes, brain and pancreas.
source: and >30 CREs have been characterised which coordinate precise spatial and temporal PAX6 expression in the developing eyes, brain and pancreas (Bhatia and Kleinjan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Successful flipping events (recombination-mediated cassette exchange) were observed at a frequency of about 10% of the injected embryos.
source: Injected embryos were scored for loss of Shh-SBE2-driven CRE activity in the forebrain and gain of mosaic eGFP and mCherry signals from the assay CRE-reporter cassette. These were scored as successful flipping events and were observed at a frequency of about 10% of the injected embryos.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations during the generation of transgenic lines.

claim: Enhancer blocking activity of the cHS4 insulator has been attributed to its ability to bind CTCF.
source: Enhancer blocking activity of this insulator has been attributed to its ability to bind CTCF (Bell et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Less than 5% variability in the reporter gene expression driven by the CREs was observed in F1 embryos derived from independent founder lines.
source: We observed <5% variability in the reporter gene expression driven by the CREs in F1 embryos derived from independent founder lines (Supplementary file 2, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations across multiple transgenic lines.

claim: Tol2 transposase mediates random integration of transgenes at Tol2 sites naturally distributed at a low frequency throughout the zebrafish genome.
source: Analysis of enhancer activities in conventional zebrafish reporter assays suffers from bias arising from position effects due to the random integration of the transgene at Tol2 sites naturally distributed at a low frequency throughout the zebrafish genome (Kawakami et al., 2000; Mann and Bhatia, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The gata2 promoter was used as the minimal promoter in both the landing pads and dual-CRE dual-reporter cassettes based on previous studies demonstrating robust promoter activity devoid of any basal level of reporter gene activation.
source: Gata2 promoter was used as the minimal promoter in both the landing pads and dual-CRE dual-reporter cassettes based on previous studies demonstrating robust promoter activity devoid of any basal level of reporter gene activation (Bhatia et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.
